newsitem.title: USA: All Cajun Electric bidders now offering cash.
newsitem.headline: All Cajun Electric bidders now offering cash.

text.p: The reorganization offers for Cajun Electric Power Cooperative Inc have all been expressed in cash.

And the number of bidders for the bankrupt power supplier 12 Louisiana distribution cooperatives has declined to three. Southern Co has joined Zeigler Coal Holding Co and Northern States Power Co in the trustee's bid.
They joined Enron Corp ; and Central and South West Corp, Entergy Corp and the Cajun Electric Members Committee group in filing amended offers.
The next step is confirmation hearings starting December 16 in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Middle District of Louisiana in Baton Rouge.
The largest bid now on the table is the one being made with the blessing of the Bankruptcy Trustee -- $1.09 billion in cash for Cajun's non-nuclear assets from Southern, Zeigler and Northern States.

It represents a combination of Southern's $1.04 billion cash offer with the $1.11 billion proposal Northern States and Zeigler put forward in April to be funded with $300 million of equity and non-recourse financing.

The members' committee, Central and South West's Southwestern Electric Power Co subsidiary and Entergy Corp's Entergy Gulf States Inc said Wednesday their amended offer called for a payment of up to $780 million in cash for Cajun's non-nuclear assets and funding of up to an additional $20 million to pay certain other bankruptcy claims and expenses.

This group had offered $405 million in cash and a payment of 5.87 mills per kilowatt hour to Cajun's largest creditor -- the Rural Utilities Service -- over 20 years. That offer was said then to have a present value of $497 to $567 million.

The amended offer calls for a Southwestern Electric affiliate to acquire the Cajun assets and enter into new 25-year power supply agreements providing the cooperatives represented by the members' committee with competitive wholesale rates starting at about 3.74 cents per kilowatt-hour.

The cooperatives also would get the flexibility to acquire additional power on the open market when their requirements exceeded mutually agreed-upon levels of generating capacity available from Southwestern.
Enron amended its previous offer to include a $750 million all cash option, spokeswoman Carol Hensley told Reuters.
She said the company's original offer of $525 million in cash and $506 million in cash flow is "still on the table."

She pointed out "We don't believe the trustee's plan has been changed by Southern joining," explaining it "still calls for a disproportionate share (of the costs) to be borne by Louisiana consumers." Enron is "confident" its proposal "is the only plan that will receive the necessary regulatory approvals," she said.

The Cajun non-nuclear assets being bid for are some 1,680 megawatts of generating capacity. This includes two, 110-megawatt natural gas fired units that make up the Big Cajun I power plant and two 575 megawatt coal fired units that are part of Big Cajun II. Cajun also has a 58 percent interest in a 540 megawatt coal-fired unit at Big Cajun II, while the other 42 percent is held by Gulf States.
Cajun's nuclear asset is a 30 percent interest in the 936 megawatt River Bend plant, which is 70 percent owned by Gulf States. -- New York Newsdesk 212-859-1610
